newsitem.title: USA: Republicans say they inching closer to budget deal.
newsitem.headline: Republicans say they inching closer to budget deal.

text.p: President Clinton and Republican lawmakers edged closer on Wednesday to a five-year plan for balancing the federal budget and cutting taxes and a key senator said he hoped it would be concluded soon.

Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott huddled with Republican colleagues to mull over the latest exchange of proposals -- most of which were communicated by telephone. White House officials outlined the plan to Democrats on Tuesday.

"The tempo has increased signficantly. We are much closer to getting agreement on a balanced budget...We are not there yet. There are gaps in a couple of critical areas," he told reporters early Wednesday evening.

But several last minute hitches developed as Republicans resisted White House demands that specifics on any tax cut be worked out as part of the overall budget agreement and not later in House and Senate tax writing committees.

Congressional tax writers want discretion to craft their own tax bill, working within broad budget parameters. The White House pushed for specific provisions on a welfare to work tax credit, the president's education plan and a range of other issues.
"They dug in their heels and started demanding specific guarantees going beyond what negotiators want," a Republican source said.

The two sides have been negotiating in secret for weeks on a plan to bring the deficit down to zero by 2002. The size of a tax cut, the depth of spending cuts and the president's request for some new programmes have been the major divisions.

The White House was still insisting on new spending for education and other domestic initiatives, Republicans said. On one major spending issue, a Democratic aide said the White House boosted its Medicare spending reduction to $115 billion from $100 billion spread over the next five years.

Clinton has said he hoped to conclude an agreement prior to his departure on Monday for Mexico. His spokesman, Mike McCurry, said while talks had been "good and productive," it was uncertain whether differences could be worked out by then.

In any case, House Democrats said they were resisting the idea of a quick deal and would prefer to take more time to negotiate a deal that included spending for their priorities of education, the environment and other domestic programmes.

House Minority Leader Dick Gephardt of Missouri praised Clinton's effort to balance the budget but said Democrats were wary of a budget deal that might hurt the Medicare health care for the elderly and wanted to see tax cuts targeted to the middle class.
"We're not going to be for a bad deal. No deal is better than a bad deal. We've got to be careful about what's agreed to here," he said at a news conference.

Senate Democratic leader Tom Daschle of South Dakota, told reporters he found reports by White House officials of the negotiations "comforting." But he warned that Republican efforts to change the way spending bills were approved would jeopardise reaching an agreement.

Democrats said they were concerned that a net tax cut of $100 billion, as crafted by Republicans with large capital gains tax rate reductions and other costly provisions, could balloon to $250 billion in the second five years.
This would either raise the deficit or force cuts in spending to pay for it.
Clinton recommended a $98 billion tax cut chiefly focused on education and child tax credits and would be paid for with $76 billion in other tax hikes for a net tax cut of $22 billion.
